identifiers.label: Main email (sample — edit or delete)
identifiers.notes: Replace with your real email, then work the Protections list.

identifiers.label: My website / domain (sample)
identifiers.notes: If you own a domain, add it here — spoofability is on the Protections list.

hardening.step: Turn on 2-step verification or a passkey for your email
hardening.why: This is the single biggest protection. Even if your password leaks, no one gets in without your second factor.
hardening.how: Gmail: Account → Security → 2-Step Verification. Prefer an authenticator app or passkey over text-message codes.

hardening.step: Use a password that is unique to your email
hardening.why: Most account takeovers come from a password reused on another site that got breached. A unique password breaks that chain.
hardening.how: Let a password manager generate and store it. Never reuse your email password anywhere else.

hardening.step: Review recent sign-in activity and connected devices
hardening.why: Shows you every device and location that logged in — the fastest way to spot an intruder.
hardening.how: Gmail: Security → Your devices, and Recent security activity. Sign out anything you don't recognize.

hardening.why: Apps you connected years ago can still read your mail or contacts and are a common quiet backdoor.
hardening.how: Google: Security → Third-party apps with account access. Revoke anything you no longer use.

hardening.why: Tells you which known data breaches your address appeared in — usually the real reason a password is floating around.
hardening.how: Visit haveibeenpwned.com, enter your email. For any breach shown, change that site's password.

hardening.why: Makes a unique strong password on every site effortless, which removes the biggest attack path.
hardening.how: Built-in options (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager) or standalone (Bitwarden, 1Password) all work.

hardening.why: If your laptop or phone is lost or stolen, encryption keeps your files and saved logins unreadable.
hardening.how: Mac: FileVault (System Settings → Privacy & Security). iPhone/Android: on by default with a passcode set.

hardening.step: Set a carrier SIM PIN / port-out lock
hardening.why: Blocks SIM-swap — where an attacker moves your number to their phone to steal text-message codes.
hardening.how: Ask your carrier to add a port-out PIN / number-transfer lock to the account.

hardening.step: Stop relying on text-message codes as your only 2FA
hardening.why: SMS codes can be intercepted or SIM-swapped. An app or passkey is much harder to steal.
hardening.how: In each account's 2FA settings, add an authenticator app or passkey and make it the default.

hardening.step: Publish a DMARC record set to reject
hardening.why: Stops strangers sending email that looks like it comes from your domain (spoofing / impersonation).
hardening.how: Add a DNS TXT record at _dmarc.yourdomain with a policy of p=reject once SPF and DKIM are in place.

hardening.step: Set up SPF and DKIM for your domain
hardening.why: They let receiving mail servers verify that mail from your domain is really yours — the foundation DMARC builds on.
hardening.how: Your email/host provider gives you the exact SPF TXT record and DKIM keys to add to DNS.

hardening.step: Force HTTPS and enable HSTS on your site
hardening.why: Ensures visitors always use the encrypted, tamper-proof version of your site.
hardening.how: Most hosts offer a one-click HTTPS + 'always redirect' toggle; add an HSTS header for the strong version.

hardening.step: Opt out of the major data-broker sites
hardening.why: People-search sites publish your name, address, phone and relatives — the raw material for scams and stalking.
hardening.how: Work the Data-broker opt-outs tab. Or use a paid removal service (DeleteMe, Optery) to do it for you.

hardening.step: Freeze your credit at the three bureaus
hardening.why: A freeze stops anyone (including a thief with your details) from opening credit in your name. It's free.
hardening.how: Request a freeze at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Unfreeze temporarily when you need new credit.

hardening.step: Use a PO box or virtual address for signups
hardening.why: Keeps your real home address out of the databases that feed data brokers in the first place.
hardening.how: Use a mailbox service or virtual address for loyalty programs, deliveries and non-essential accounts.

guides.topic: How your info actually leaks (most common first)
guides.body: 1) Data breach + password reuse — your password leaked from some OTHER site and was tried on your email. This is by far the most common, and touches neither your computer nor your wifi. 2) Phishing — you typed details into a fake login page. 3) Malware on your device recording what you type. 4) Wifi sniffing — the scary-sounding one, but modern sites use HTTPS so your password is encrypted before it leaves your device; a hostile wifi's real trick is redirecting you to a fake page (that's phishing again). Bottom line: a stolen password usually means a breach somewhere, not a hacked Mac.

guides.topic: What this app can and cannot scan
guides.body: Honest limits. Emails and passwords CAN be checked against known breaches — but only with the optional advanced setup (a paid data source + your server), which is not turned on yet. Websites/domains CAN be checked for spoofability and HTTPS — also part of the optional advanced setup. Names and addresses CANNOT be reliably auto-scanned by anyone; the real defense is the opt-out tracker and hardening list in this app. Anything claiming a live 'name scan' is mostly guessing.

guides.topic: Email spoofing and DMARC, in plain words
guides.body: If you own a domain, strangers can send email that looks like it's from you unless you tell the world how to tell real from fake. Three DNS records do this: SPF lists who may send for you, DKIM signs your mail, and DMARC says 'reject anything that fails'. With all three set to reject, impersonation from your domain stops. Your email/hosting provider gives you the exact records to paste in.

guides.topic: SIM-swap: why your phone is weak 2FA
guides.body: A SIM-swap is when someone convinces your carrier to move your number to their phone. Then every text-message security code goes to them. Two defenses: add a port-out PIN / transfer lock with your carrier, and switch your important accounts from SMS codes to an authenticator app or passkey.

People-search sites scrape public records and sell your name, address, phone and relatives. Opting out is free but tedious — each site has its own form (see the Data-broker opt-outs tab). Expect to repeat it every 6–12 months as they re-list you. If that's too much work, paid services like DeleteMe or Optery run the opt-outs for you on a subscription.

guides.topic: Advanced checks (optional — not set up yet)
guides.body: A future upgrade can add live checks: which breaches your email appears in, whether a specific password is in leaked lists, a website's security headers, and phone validation. These have to run on your own server because they need a paid Have-I-Been-Pwned key and because browsers block these calls for safety. Nothing here is built or turned on yet — it's a deliberate, separate step for when you decide the paid data source is worth it. The free workbook you're using now needs none of that.
